trajectory_summary: The call opens with an immediate cost objection, moves through a cascade of personal disclosures (husband's death, financial exploitation, isolation, age/legacy concerns, and finally home condition), and ends with the rep withdrawing the offer and closing the call politely. Energy leaked steadily as the customer stacked real, distinct barriers that the rep never fully engaged with individually — he stayed in generic pitch mode through most of the call and only conceded at the very end.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep never asked for or received a specific bill amount or usage figure; the conversation stayed at the level of general cost/savings framing without ever anchoring to her actual dollar number.

bill_document_audit.reasoning: The call never reached bill/utility document collection — it ended in the verify/objection-handling stage before any bill-collection ask was made.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: vulnerability disclosure handling — stay with the person, not the pitch
primary_coaching_focus.quote: I mean, I I've been looking at it for since my husband died five years ago.
primary_coaching_focus.why: This customer stacked three distinct hardship disclosures (bereavement/exploitation, isolation/financial strain, home condition) inside a five-minute call, and the rep's responses stayed at 'gotcha' / 'I understand' level each time instead of naming what she'd actually shared. This is the single biggest gap on this call — not the close, the human read.

key_moments.quote: Oh, I mean, we take care of the upfront cost, so there's nothing out of your pocket.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer's stated barrier ('I can't afford solar') is exactly the situation the objection_inversion play is built for — flipping to 'what you can't afford is your current bill.' The rep instead explains the financing mechanism (no upfront cost) rather than reframing her framing.
